before: According to the old law's arrangement, the royal and the priestly classes were different; after that arrangement, the gospel received one and the same priest and king teaching. For Christ is both; since these have been so built up, it is necessary for those sown by him, while both king and priest exist in him, to be an elect race becoming both a kingdom and a priesthood. For he who begot both possessing the principles of both, it is necessary that they also be as from a king, royal, and as from a priest, a priesthood; therefore they are also called a holy nation, being called from the one who is holy and calling to 'you shall be holy' (Ex 19:6). The same are a holy nation and also a people for the preservation of all having become outside of all destruction; for preservation is of those being taken in, not of those being cast out. Since those called from different nations and laws have cast off all variety in taking up one mind, one faith and teaching, through which soul and heart become one, they are one holy nation.

Since therefore I am in this disposition toward you, to whom I write the letter, I exhort and urge you to abstain from the pleasures growing from the flesh; for these wage war against the soul, having much hatred toward it, especially since the essence of the soul and the flesh are different.

Regarding human creation, it speaks of the principles being ordained by kings; therefore it is necessary to be subject to these through the Lord; but if through the Lord we are being made subject to the one saying: 'Render to Caesar the things of Caesar' (Mt 22:21), when they command something outside the will of the Lord, let us not obey.

It does not recommend having a passive fear toward masters by the servants—for this is irrational and exists even in irrational animals—but rather that which comes with knowledge and right reason; whose master's name is reverence. For the one fearing a master through Christ and his teaching submits to him with reverence, [unlike] the one fearing a master through wickedness and other tortures, having a passive [fear].
He uses this to signify fear, and also says something else toward the women: 'watching'—that is, the men—'your conduct which is pure in fear'; for this is customary in much of the divine scripture.

Women are exhorted to imitate the holy ones, and especially Sarah, persuading them to subject themselves to their husbands just as she did to Abraham, of whom he says they become her children because of doing good works; for just as someone doing the works of Abraham and having his faith becomes his child, so women practicing good things have Sarah as a mother. Therefore, these things should be applied to the mother of those born according to the spirit, the upper Jerusalem, whom he prepared the women to have as Sarah for a mother through good works.

before: The disciples show that, since God exists as light, there is no darkness in him. We offer this same message to you, so that you may have the same glory concerning God as existing light; for God is an intelligible, eternal light; for nothing sensible exists perpetually. Regarding this light, one must understand darkness as ignorance and a deficiency of control, since neither of the forms of darkness—neither ignorance nor evil—is in God; thus it is rightly said that there is no darkness in him.
If it is said anywhere, 'the darkness of his hiding,' darkness here refers to the obscurity found in incomprehensibility; and our ignorance may be that obscurity, but not the light of God being such.

To know in the Scripture does not always signify merely to have certain knowledge, but also to have experienced something and to be united to it, as in: 'not knowing sin' (1 John 3:8), and: 'I never knew you, workers of lawlessness' (Matthew 7:23); for he did not know sin as in not having certain knowledge of what sin is, but as in not having practiced it. Therefore, he who says he has known God must necessarily follow by being transformed by him and participating in him by keeping his commandments; thus he contradicts himself. The two meanings of knowing are made clear from the context; for he says, 'by this we know' (1 John 2:3), that is, we have certain knowledge, 'that we have known him' (1 John 2:3) by being united to him and keeping his commandments; for he who does not keep them is clearly found outside the knowledge of God.

Just as our Lord Jesus, being the fullness of wisdom and truth existing as God, is not deprived of not knowing sin or the workers of lawlessness, so also [he is not deprived of] not knowing the day of judgment. It is not diminished, not even, when it is said of God that he has forgetfulness, regret, or anger, for by that word those things are made clear, and by that word also concerning the unknown...

That the day might be released; for just as in the only wise God, who possesses the knowledge of all things, there exists no forgetfulness or regret or anything of that kind—as is said economically concerning Him—so also, since the ignorance of the wisdom and truth of God is not accepted, it is usefully stated that he is ignorant of the hour and the day of judgment. Truly, he speaks of a perfect love, from which the one contained by it cannot be separated from any of the evils or deceits.

Perhaps someone will say: how is it possible to understand the written commandment concerning love to be from the beginning and to have been heard by those to whom the epistle is written? For they were not Jews, as the end of the epistle demonstrates; for he says, 'Little children, keep yourselves from idols' (1 John 5:21). Therefore, is the commandment, existing from the beginning and heard by all men, a friendly disposition according to natural concepts? For all, being by nature diurnal and social animals, love their neighbors; whence the Savior, stirring up this natural disposition, says: 'Therefore, all that you wish that men would do to you, do likewise to them' (Matt 7:12).

So that no one might think the system of those in heaven and earth and those in them to be present here from the voice of the world, he interpreted what 'those in it' turns out to be, so that we too might accordingly receive it; for 'and those in it' signifies a passion and a material disposition indicated through the desire of the flesh, which wages war against the soul, and the lust of the eyes (1 John 2:16).

It is also possible from what has been set forth to derive a view concerning the visible world, which is no longer loved by those who have ascended to seeing not the temporal things, but the eternal things; and since those who prefer to love life in it handle the sensible things passively, it is appropriately stated that in it there is the arrogance of life, of the flesh, and the lust of the eyes.

before: The good-doer, in practice and in contemplation, having God — Christ — existing as the true light, is far from darkness and from Beliar. But since doing evil is the opposite of doing good, the evil-doer, by this very activity, being of Beliar and of darkness, has not seen God nor has any knowledge of him: “for everyone who sins has not seen God nor known him” (1 John 3:6). Since seeing a body or not seeing it is recognized by using sight or not using it — the sensible object being seen by the evil-doer too, if he has sight, but not seen by the one deprived of sight, even if he be a good-doer — it is shown indisputably by the same things together: that to the good-doer, because he has a pure heart, he is seen, even if he lacks sight; but he is not seen by the evil-doer, even if he be most sharp-sighted. He presents that doing good and doing evil are opposites and therefore incompatible, both from “turn away from evil and do good” (Ps 36:27) and from the passages written similarly.

Some impious men, having plied the divine teaching with flattery and sorcery, slipped in by feigning it — “written beforehand,” that is, foreknown, for this judgment, which they judged among themselves, having been delivered over to a reprobate mind. These, being licentious through exceeding impiety, turned the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ into lasciviousness, and by the very act of wantonness denying the only Master Jesus Christ, the Lord of those called through the gospel. Then, in order to turn the faithful away from such evil and impious men, he shows how great […].

before: According to the old law's arrangement, the royal and the priestly classes were different; after that arrangement, the gospel received one and the same priest and king teaching. For Christ is both; since these have been so built up, it is necessary for those sown by him, while both king and priest exist in him, to be an elect race becoming both a kingdom and a priesthood. For he who begot both possessing the principles of both, it is necessary that they also be as from a king, royal, and as from a priest, a priesthood; therefore they are also called a holy nation, being called from the one who is holy and calling to 'you shall be holy' (Ex 19:6). The same are a holy nation and also a people for the preservation of all having become outside of all destruction; for preservation is of those being taken in, not of those being cast out. Since those called from different nations and laws have cast off all variety in taking up one mind, one faith and teaching, through which soul and heart become one, they are one holy nation.

Those who through godliness are found worthy of being obeyed are appropriately loved by those who desire them humanly, but they are not being loved [as truly loved]. Since therefore I am in this disposition toward you, to whom I write the letter, I exhort and urge you to abstain from the pleasures growing from the flesh; for these wage war against the soul, having much hatred toward it, especially since the essence of the soul and the flesh are different.

Regarding human creation, it speaks of the principles being ordained by kings; therefore it is necessary to be subject to these through the Lord; but if through the Lord we are being made subject to the one saying: 'Render to Caesar the things of Caesar' (Mt 22:21), when they command something outside the will of the Lord, let us not obey.

It does not recommend having a passive fear toward masters by the servants—for this is irrational and exists even in irrational animals—but rather that which comes with knowledge and right reason; whose master's name is reverence. For the one fearing a master through Christ and his teaching submits to him with reverence, [unlike] the one fearing a master through wickedness and other tortures, having a passive [fear].
He uses this to signify fear, and also says something else toward the women: 'watching'—that is, the men—'your conduct which is pure in fear'; for this is customary in much of the divine scripture.

Women are exhorted to imitate the holy ones, and especially Sarah, persuading them to subject themselves to their husbands just as she did to Abraham, of whom he says they become her children because of doing good works; for just as someone doing the works of Abraham and having his faith becomes his child, so women practicing good things have Sarah as a mother. But observe toward allegory how one becomes a child of Abraham and Sarah; according to the apostle, Abraham had two sons, one from the slave girl and one from the free woman; then, having led them into the two covenants, he says with something else that the latter became free according to the spirit, having spoken of the upper Jerusalem (Galatians 3:16). This agrees with: 'look to Abraham your father and to Sarah who was in labor for you' (Isaiah 51:2); for it is not possible to refer these things to them; for how could she, who owed death by nature many generations ago, still be in labor at the time of the prophet? Therefore, these things should be applied to the mother of those born according to the spirit, the upper Jerusalem, whom he prepared the women to have as Sarah for a mother through good works.

'And sanctify the Lord God in your hearts.' Just as magnifying God does not imply adding greatness to Him, nor does glorifying Him imply bringing fame to Him from without, so neither does sanctifying the Lord mean adding holiness to Him; which is what we are commanded to do in our own heart. For if we were to hold a precise discussion of His holiness, we would not at all be adding to Him, but rather, by doing this in our heart, we add to our own understanding the holiness concerning God; likewise, he who magnifies Him receives a participation in His own greatness; whence it is said: 'my soul magnifies the Lord' (Luke 1:46) and: 'magnify the Lord with me' (Psalm 34:3); likewise, he who knows glory glorifies Him into himself; and these things do not seem paradoxical to one who knows accurately how God does not receive [additions], but...
